claims.text: The initial equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloy is single-phase FCC.
The initial FeCoNi-based alloy has high saturation magnetization.
The initial FeCoNi-based alloy has low coercivity.
Substitution with up to approximately 10 at.% Sn will promote partial transformation of the FCC matrix toward BCC or stabilize BCC nanoprecipitates.
Sn introduces local lattice distortions in the FCC matrix.
The Sn-induced lattice distortions favor a secondary BCC structural motif.
The emergent BCC regions have higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy than the FCC matrix.
BCC regions or nanoprecipitates provide effective domain-wall-pinning sites.
Increased magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain-wall pinning will increase coercivity.
The Sn-modified alloy will have higher coercivity than predominantly FCC FeCoNi, FeCoNiPd, and FeCoNiPt baselines.
The Sn-modified alloy will retain high saturation magnetization while its coercivity increases.
Previously reported FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives are soft magnetic and primarily FCC.
The beneficial coercivity effect is expected only for minor Sn substitutions up to roughly 10 at.%.
Sn levels above roughly 10 at.% may cause excessive phase separation.
Sn levels above roughly 10 at.% may degrade magnetic and mechanical properties.
The effectiveness of Sn substitution depends on homogeneous mixing and processing conditions that permit FCC–BCC coexistence.
Earlier observations in related FeCoNi systems show that Sn additions promote BCC phase formation.
The modified alloy must retain a configurational entropy of at least 1.0R.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes replacing one Fe, Co, or Ni constituent with 0–10 at.% Sn while remaining only near-equiatomic, whereas the experiment calls every member of the 0, 2, 5, and 10 at.% Sn series equiatomic. A four-element alloy with 2–10 at.% Sn cannot be fully equiatomic across Fe, Co, Ni, and Sn, and no exact recipe resolves the terminology.
